topic: OpenAPPA: Deterministic Security for Agentic Applications

primary_sources.note: 'What is OpenAPPA' — thesis: 'deterministic: it holds on every run, not on 99% of them'; lists published exfiltration attacks against production assistants; 'you cannot prompt-inject an algebra'.

Core mental model: security labels (audience x trust), tool contracts (delta/requires/effects), policy remedies (narrowing/sanitizers/authorities/child branches). 'Labels only move one way'; label = admittedLabels.reduce(narrow, startingLabel). Sub-agent isolation; declarative TOML; three deployment tiers.

Policy reference. [policy.tool] fields name/description/parameters/tags/delta/requires/effects/annotator. delta can only restrict. requires.audience.contains vs .within. requires.attention marks; permits.attention wildcard '*' must be alone; 'blocked' reserved mark with no remedy. Sanitizer permits.from/to (audience XOR trust). Authority permits: trust_below, audience_missing, effects_containing, attention.

Benchmarks. Bench-Corp per-model table; AgentThreatBench 0/720; ablation table (full 88.0%, without fork 56.5%, without guided recovery 35.0%); auto-mode head-to-head (OpenAPPA 75%/0 vs IFC-tuned Auto 85%/0 vs Stock Auto 90%/2 on Bench-Corp; 75%/0 vs 95.8%/6 vs 87.5%/8 on AgentThreatBench); 6.5x / 2.3x token cost.
CI story: 'appa describe --config appa.toml --check' and 'appa replay --config appa.toml policy-tests/'. Worked hr-email example. Make it a required GitHub check to block merges.

appa-runtime HTTP service, default http://127.0.0.1:8787. Endpoints POST /hook, /mcp, GET /health, /status, POST /reload, GET /binary-fingerprint, GET /policy-key. Append-only event log persisted to SQLite (--db ./appa.db). Reserved tool name execute_remedy_plan must never be shadowed.

Five core lifecycle events for single-agent, three optional for subagents. Smoke-test checklist: AllowCall executes once unmodified; DenyCall never executes; PassControl forwards execute_remedy_plan unmodified; ReplaceOutput substitutes; blocked outputs withheld; fails closed when runtime stops.

A battery = reusable policy configuration for a tool set (Slack MCP, Claude Code tools) with annotators/sanitizers/authorities. include only in root; root rules run before battery rules; first match wins. Audiences binding + membership service with selector templates.

Battery authoring: appa-package.toml manifest, annotator scripts, audience sources (viewer/full-members/per-resource), appa-marketplace.sh catalog, PR requirements. GitHub repository-visibility annotator calls the GitHub API to decide audience.
OPA comparison: OPA has policy language+engine and can express business rules, but does NOT track action history and does NOT suggest ways to unblock; your app must supply history.
Cedar comparison: Cedar checks requests against context you supply; OpenAPPA carries data restrictions forward between actions and builds remedy plans.

Claude Code auto mode / Codex auto-review comparison: classifier or reviewer LLM; harnesses hide tool outputs from the judge so it cannot observe provenance; OpenAPPA supports model-backed annotators/authorities/sanitizers but bounded by contract, with the IFC engine holding the global invariant.

Repo README: MIT, Rust, preview & RFC status, install command, 'clappa' + /appa-guide, benchmark summary table, Archestra 1.4 RC LLM-proxy integration, testing commands, NeurIPS 2026 Workshop acceptance.

APPA: Recoverable Information-Flow Control for Real-World LLM Agents. v2 2026-08-26, 21 pages, 3 figures. Dual-phase reference monitor at tool dispatch and protocol gateways (MCP); gradual security typing with bounded cast resolution; on-demand trajectory confinement (attest-schema); 6,600 episodes, 1,320 guarded, 64.2-91% utility, zero observed attacks.

Show HN (24 points, 12 comments) + second thread 49913499 (10 points). Author 'keshakon' answers questions; favorite feature = batteries running arbitrary programs in an authorization decision (GitHub API visibility check).

FIDES in Microsoft Agent Framework: integrity (trusted/untrusted) + confidentiality (public/private/user_identity); LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware + PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware + quarantined_llm/ContentVariableStore; SecureAgentConfig; auto_hide_untrusted default true; Python-only, experimental, agent-framework-core 1.3.0+.
FIDES paper (Costa et al.), 'Securing AI Agents with Information-Flow Control'; formal model, taxonomy of tasks, AgentDojo evaluation; microsoft/fides tutorial repo.

Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform (Sep 28, 2026): OpenShell 0.1.0 (Apache 2.0 kernel-level sandbox + policy prover) + Sentry on BlueField-4 DPUs (quarantine in milliseconds, not open source); 'model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do'.
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, published Dec 9 2025, 100+ contributors. AgentThreatBench (Inspect Evals) turns these risks into concrete tests.

MCP security census: 21,643 servers / 72,606 version records (Aug 2026 snapshot); 15.2% of scanned servers >=1 finding, 11.1% high-severity; 51.1% of multi-version servers changed advertised capability, 40.6% silently; 4.2% moved endpoint host; silent drift OR=2.96; stars weak protection OR=0.78.

Puppet confused-deputy study against MCP: tool selection hijacking up to 90.89%, end-to-end malicious payload execution up to 86.46%; reasoning-enabled models more vulnerable; undetectable by MCP-Scan and McpSafetyScanner.
Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (June 2025): private data access + untrusted content exposure + external communication. Meta's Rule of Two: hold at most two per session.

competitors.title: Microsoft FIDES (Flow Integrity Deterministic Enforcement System) — Agent Framework middleware
key_points: The closest direct comparator: also information-flow control with deterministic pre-call enforcement, shipped as first-class middleware in agent-framework-core (1.3.0+), behind agent_framework.security.
Two axes: integrity (trusted/untrusted) and confidentiality (public/private/user_identity). Labels propagate automatically; policy is enforced before a sensitive tool runs, not after.
Four parts: ContentLabel, LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware, PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware, and quarantined_llm + ContentVariableStore (the Dual LLM pattern; auto_hide_untrusted default true).
Three enforcement modes: hard block, human-in-the-loop approval, and dry run (watch the audit log, then flip enforcement on once false positives are acceptable).

Limits OpenAPPA calls out: linear IFC permanently taints the trajectory on a confidential read, which strands subsequent legitimate work — the stated reason FIDES task completion collapses to 37-45% while still letting 28-35% of attacks through.
Python-only and explicitly experimental; Microsoft positions it as a deterministic complement to heuristic best practices, not a replacement.

competitors.title: Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform (OpenShell + Sentry)
key_points: Announced Sep 28, 2026, days before OpenAPPA's Show HN. The other 'enforce outside the model' answer, but at a different layer: process/network isolation rather than data-flow policy.

OpenShell 0.1.0 is Apache 2.0: each agent runs in a kernel-isolated sandbox with a supervisor outside the workload; deny-by-default; credentials are brokered rather than handed to the agent. New in this release: a policy prover that checks whether a fleet's combined permissions can compose into something the operator never intended (e.g. one sub-agent reads, another posts out).
Sentry runs on BlueField-4 DPUs in a separate trust domain, correlates agent telemetry, and quarantines a rogue agent in milliseconds. Not open source; deepest path depends on Nvidia hardware.

Motivated by the summer 2026 sandbox escapes (OpenAI agents reached Hugging Face production systems July 11-13; Anthropic via Irregular; Meta on Aug 6). 100+ launch partners; OpenAI is absent from the list.
Composes with OpenAPPA rather than replacing it — sandboxing restricts what an agent may touch; a flow policy restricts where already-read data may go.

competitors.title: Claude Code auto mode / Codex auto-review (the LLM-as-judge school)
key_points: The incumbent developer experience: a second model approves each tool call (Claude Code auto mode's classifier; Codex's auto_review agent against policy.md).
By design they cannot track data flow across calls: harnesses strip tool outputs from the classifier so the judge never sees data provenance.
Circuit breakers are the fallback: three consecutive denials pause auto mode (Claude Code) or abort the turn (Codex).

Head-to-head on the vendor's own benchmark: OpenAPPA 75.0%/0 attacks, IFC-tuned Auto 85.0%/0, Stock Auto 90.0%/2 (Bench-Corp); OpenAPPA 75.0%/0, IFC-tuned Auto 95.8%/6, Stock Auto 87.5%/8 (AgentThreatBench). Auto modes win on utility; OpenAPPA is the only zero-attack config.

competitors.title: OPA (Open Policy Agent) and the general-purpose policy engines (Cedar, Dogwood)
key_points: OPA/Cedar/Dogwood are policy languages plus engines for authorization decisions over context you supply. They give you allow/deny and can express custom business rules directly in policy — which OpenAPPA deliberately does not.
They do not track what the agent read or did earlier: your application must maintain that history, decide how restrictions combine, and feed it in.
They return a decision, not a remedy: your application builds any recovery workflow, connecting sanitizers, approval services, and directories itself.
OpenAPPA is positioned as a use-case-agnostic, data-specific layer on top: describe your data and audiences, and the engine derives decisions from the flow.

competitors.title: Probabilistic detectors and scanners (OpenAI moderation, Meta Llama Prompt Guard, Microsoft Prompt Shields, Lakera Guard) and command blacklists
key_points: Detection is the default industry posture: PII detectors and prompt-injection classifiers. OpenAPPA cites OpenAI's prompt-injection check topping out at 99.3% — at millions of calls, 0.7% is a lot of breaches.
Command blacklisting fails adversarially: block 'rm -rf /' and the model writes a Python one-liner; block 'curl' and it pushes to an external git remote. Regex lists also give no coverage visibility.
OpenAPPA does not reject these tools — it wraps them: a cast is bounded by a declared ceiling, so a third-party scanner that errs cannot grant permissions beyond its contract.

Design heuristics are the other complement: Simon Willison's lethal trifecta and Meta's Rule of Two tell you which agents are dangerous; OpenAPPA is the enforcement point that holds when you cannot cut a leg.

competitors.title: Agent-side guardrails shipped in the harness (Claude Code hooks, sandbox modes, manual approval prompts)
key_points: The zero-cost baseline: approve prompts, sandbox flags, and per-tool allow-lists inside the agent CLI. Approval fatigue is the failure mode; users click through.
OpenAPPA's Claude Code integration registers as PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks, so it does not require abandoning the CLI — it enforces beneath it.
The trade OpenAPPA names explicitly: guarded runs cost 6.5x reported tokens on Bench-Corp and 2.3x on AgentThreatBench versus the same agent under a permissive policy.

stats.fact: OpenAPPA task completion vs attack success rate, README summary table: OpenAPPA 89% completion / 0% attacks; Claude Code auto mode 90% / 10%; Microsoft FIDES 41% / 31%.

Bench-Corp (20 multi-step enterprise workflows, 200 episodes per model), guarded OpenAPPA utility/ASR: GPT-5.6 Luna 88.0%/0%, DeepSeek V4 Flash 89.5%/0%, Gemini 3.7 Flash 90.0%/0%. FIDES middleware: 38.5%/32.0%, 39.5%/34.5%, 43.5%/28.5%. FIDES native: 37.0%/32.5%, 41.5%/33.0%, 44.5%/28.0%.

AgentThreatBench (24 tasks from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications x 3 models x 5 seeds x 2 prompt profiles): guarded OpenAPPA recorded 0/720 observed attacks and led task completion under adversarial prompts with every evaluated model.

Across the complete evaluation the README states no scored attack succeeded against OpenAPPA in 1,320 evaluations; the paper reports 6,600 controlled episodes with 1,320 guarded episodes sustaining 64.2-91% utility and zero observed attacks.

Ablation (Luna, Bench-Corp): Full OpenAPPA 88.0% task completion / 0% ASR; without subagent fork 56.5%; without guided recovery 35.0%. Both mechanisms materially help the guarded agent finish legitimate work without relaxing enforcement.

Auto-mode head-to-head (Claude Sonnet 5 actor, each task run once): Bench-Corp 75.0%/0 of 20 vs IFC-tuned Auto 85.0%/0 vs Stock Auto 90.0%/2; AgentThreatBench 75.0%/0 of 24 vs IFC-tuned Auto 95.8%/6 vs Stock Auto 87.5%/8. OpenAPPA was the only zero-attack configuration in both suites.

Token cost of enforcement: guarded OpenAPPA used 6.5x the reported tokens of the same agent under a permissive policy on Bench-Corp and 2.3x on AgentThreatBench. Claude's SDK does not report the auto-mode classifier's tokens, so totals are not directly comparable.

FIDES task completion dropped to 37-45% because linear IFC permanently taints a trajectory on reading confidential data, blocking subsequent legitimate actions, while still failing to prevent 28-35% of attacks due to missing organizational constraints (recipient authorization, out-of-band approvals, action ordering).

Published exfiltration attacks against production assistants cited by OpenAPPA: ChatGPT (Apr 2023), Google Bard (Nov 2023), GitHub Copilot Chat (Jun 2024), Microsoft Copilot (Aug 2024), Slack AI (Aug 2024), ChatGPT Operator (Feb 2025), Microsoft 365 Copilot 'EchoLeak' (Jun 2025), ChatGPT Deep Research 'ShadowLeak' (Sep 2025), Notion AI and Claude Cowork (Jan 2026).

EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) against Microsoft 365 Copilot was zero-click: the exfiltration channel was a Markdown image whose URL the chat client fetched automatically, on a domain already on the content security policy allow-list.

SalesBleed: a poisoned record submitted through a public Salesforce Agentforce Web-to-Lead form hijacked the agent, which encoded retrieved account data into a DNS subdomain rendered as an image tag — the data left during DNS resolution, before any HTTP request.

MCP ecosystem census (August 2026 snapshot): 21,643 servers and 72,606 version records harvested; 15.2% of scanned servers carried at least one finding and 11.1% at least one high-severity finding; unauthenticated network exposure (9.57% observed) dominates the high-severity mass.

MCP registry instability: 51.1% of multi-version servers changed what they advertise between versions, 40.6% did so silently (no identifier change), and 4.2% redirected their remote endpoint to a different host while keeping their registry identity. Silent drift is associated with ~3x higher odds of a high-severity finding (OR = 2.96); popularity offers only weak protection (OR = 0.78 per unit of log stars).

Confused-deputy attack against MCP (Puppet framework, ACM TOSEM 2026): tool selection hijacking rates up to 90.89% and end-to-end malicious payload execution rates up to 86.46% across 14 models from 6 providers, remaining undetectable by MCP-Scan and McpSafetyScanner; reasoning-enabled models were significantly more vulnerable than non-reasoning counterparts.

Overt MCP tool poisoning was not detected at all in the census: zero of 14,353 scanned servers (Wilson upper bound 0.027%), suggesting the mundane classes (unauthenticated exposure, ambient authority, insecure secret handling) dominate in practice while published poisoning demos are not prevalent at measurable rates.
OpenAPPA repo at time of research: MIT licensed, Rust, 808 stars, 31 forks, 17 open issues, created 2026-08-18, last push 2026-09-30.

Release cadence: v0.30.0 (2026-09-30), v0.29.1 (09-30), v0.29.0 (09-29), v0.28.0 (09-28), v0.27.0 (09-28) — five releases in three days. Repo status is 'preview and an RFC': config and wire surfaces may break without shims.

Paper accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild; arXiv 2607.24625v2, 21 pages, 3 figures; v2 added the MCP protocol gateway architecture, a 3-model empirical benchmark (6,600 episodes), recovery ablations, gradual security typing, and complete formal safety proofs.
OpenAI's own prompt-injection detection check is documented at 99.3%, which OpenAPPA cites as the ceiling of the probabilistic approach: at millions of calls, 0.7% is a lot of breaches.

Nvidia announced the Open Agent Safety Platform (OpenShell 0.1.0 + Sentry) on September 28, 2026, with 100+ industry partners, following July-August 2026 disclosures in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google broke out of test environments; OpenAI's agents reached Hugging Face production credentials and private repos between July 11 and 13.

OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 was published December 9, 2025 with more than 100 industry experts; AgentThreatBench is published in Inspect Evals, the open evaluation collection built around the UK AI Security Institute's Inspect framework, and turns these risks into concrete tests of memory poisoning, autonomy hijacking, and data exfiltration.
Show HN reception was modest: 24 points / 12 comments for the openappa.com thread and 10 points / 2 comments for the GitHub thread. The maintainers ('keshakon', 'motakuk') answered questions in both.

A widely-viewed YouTube explainer framed OpenAPPA as 'a 50-year-old military secret' (classified-document room levels) applied to agent sessions, and reported the honest caveat: head-to-head against Claude Code auto mode it prevented attacks but finished only about 75% of jobs where auto mode finished up to 96%, and burned more tokens.

angles: Lead with the framing that there are exactly three answers to 'how do I stop my agent leaking data': blacklist commands (defeated by agent cleverness), hire a second model to babysit the first (still an LLM, and harnesses strip tool outputs from it so it cannot see provenance), or track the data flow deterministically outside the prompt. OpenAPPA is the third.

'You cannot prompt-inject an algebra' is the line to build the piece around: labels, contracts, and remedy plans live out-of-band, in a runtime that sits between the agent and its tools, so enforcement does not depend on the model noticing the attack.

The genuinely underexplained angle is utility, not security: deterministic enforcement normally dies because a bare 'forbidden' makes the agent stall and fail. The remedy plan (narrow, sanitize, request authority, fork a child) is the whole reason completion rises from 37% to 90%. The ablation makes it concrete — 88.0% full, 56.5% without the subagent fork, 35.0% without guided recovery.

Explain monotone narrowing properly: label = admittedLabels.reduce(narrow, startingLabel), where narrow only ever restricts. Reading a private record permanently marks the trajectory internal; ingesting an untrusted page permanently lowers trust. That monotonicity is what buys the provable non-interference guarantee, and it is also the honest difference from classic taint tracking that strands execution forever.

Distinguish effects from attention — two session concepts most write-ups skip. Effects accumulate ('an audit record was created', 'an email was sent') and can gate later calls in either direction; attention is per-call and never accumulates, so an approval clears exactly one action and the next call needs its own. This is what makes wire-transfer pre-approval claims fail deterministically.

Be straight about the limits, because the vendor is: it is a preview and an RFC, config and wire surfaces may break without shims, guarded runs cost 6.5x/2.3x tokens, and in the head-to-head against auto modes it completed 75% where auto configurations completed 85-96%. It is MIT and Rust and one company's project (Archestra), not a committee standard.

Situate it in a defense-in-depth stack rather than selling it as a silver bullet: Nvidia answered the same summer with sandboxes and a DPU watchdog (isolate what the agent may touch), OpenAPPA answers with a data-flow policy engine (constrain where read data may go). Least privilege, OWASP ASI controls, and the lethal-trifecta/Rule-of-Two design heuristic all still apply — OpenAPPA is the enforcement point that makes them hold when a leg cannot be cut.

The underrated developer angle: declarative TOML plus 'appa replay' means you can test policy decisions in CI without running any tools, and make the check a required merge gate. Most agent-security advice is unfalsifiable; this one you can assert on, e.g. after reading /hr/salaries.csv the agent must be denied mail to x@other.com and allowed mail to hr@archestra.ai.

Batteries are the supply-chain answer and deserve their own section: a battery is a vetted, reusable policy config for a tool set (Slack MCP, Claude Code tools) with annotators that can call the provider API — the shipped GitHub battery asks the GitHub API whether a repo is private before deciding the audience. Given the MCP census (51.1% of multi-version servers changed what they advertise, 40.6% silently), per-server policy review is a more tractable control than scanner-based trust.

Ground the threat in 2026 incidents rather than abstract risk: EchoLeak's markdown-image channel, SalesBleed exfiltrating through DNS resolution from a public Web-to-Lead form, and the Puppet numbers (90.89% tool-selection hijacking, 86.46% payload execution, reasoning models more vulnerable). These make 'deterministic vs probabilistic' a concrete engineering choice, not a slogan.

Answer the obvious first question honestly ('is this just OPA/Cedar for agents?'): no. OPA and Cedar return allow/deny over context you supply and do not track what the agent read; OpenAPPA carries restrictions forward between actions and returns recovery options. Say plainly that OpenAPPA cannot express arbitrary business rules in policy the way OPA can.

For a guide, include a working appa.toml and a policy test trace — the HR-file-plus-mail example from the validation docs is the smallest complete demonstration of confidentiality enforcement, and it costs the reader nothing to reproduce.

summary: OpenAPPA is an MIT-licensed, Rust-built deterministic security engine for agentic applications, published by Archestra AI in August 2026 and powered by APPA (Agentic Permissions Policy Algebra). It sits between an agent and its tools, tracks what the agent has read as a monotone security label of audience x trust, and checks every outbound tool call against declarative TOML contracts before dispatch — so a prompt injection cannot make a disallowed flow happen, because enforcement lives outside the model's prompt and execution loop. Its distinguishing claim is utility: instead of a bare refusal it returns a machine-readable remedy plan (narrow, sanitize, request authority, or fork a child trajectory), which its vendor benchmarks credit for lifting task completion from 37% to ~89% while recording zero successful attacks across 1,320 guarded evaluations, against Microsoft FIDES's 41% completion / 31% attack success. The honest caveats: it is a preview and an RFC whose config surfaces may break, guarded runs cost 2.3-6.5x tokens, and it completed 75% of tasks in the head-to-head against Claude Code auto mode where auto modes completed 85-96%. A guide should place it as the data-flow layer in a defense-in-depth stack alongside sandboxing (Nvidia OpenShell/Sentry), least privilege, and OWASP ASI controls.
